query: Eutectic high-entropy alloys contain dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries, where microcracking can initiate and lead to catastrophic damage during room-temperature tensile deformation. Conventional processing commonly raises strength at the expense of ductility, while the wide range of previously proposed microstructural-design and processing strategies has not eliminated room-temperature brittleness and limited tensile ductility. Under these constraints, what single intervention could improve both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility? State one testable hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introduction of a controlled amount of lattice distortion through cryogenic thermal cycling can improve both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility in eutectic high-entropy alloys.
generation.material_initial_state: Dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries in eutectic high-entropy alloys
generation.structural_mediator: Lattice distortion and altered dislocation dynamics
generation.mechanism: The introduction of lattice distortion through cryogenic thermal cycling can alter dislocation dynamics, potentially reducing the propensity for microcracking at internal boundaries and enhancing ductility while maintaining or increasing strength due to the refined microstructure and increased lattice friction.
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved strength and room-temperature tensile ductility compared to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline
generation.boundary: The intervention's effectiveness is bounded by the alloy's composition, the extent of lattice distortion introduced, and the number of thermal cycles
generation.uncertainty: The optimal amount of lattice distortion and the precise mechanism by which cryogenic thermal cycling affects dislocation dynamics and microcracking are uncertain and require further investigation

falsification_experiment.design: Compare the room-temperature tensile properties of eutectic high-entropy alloys subjected to cryogenic thermal cycling with those of unmodified alloys
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the cryogenically cycled alloys do not exhibit a significant improvement in both strength and ductility compared to the unmodified alloys, the hypothesis is falsified

cited_evidence.text: We believe that the combination of yield strength, tensile strength and tensile ductility displayed by the W-based refractory HEA with the SCCPs structure is superior to previously reported tungsten-based, Ni-based superalloys, and refractory HEAs (Fig. 3b).

Developing alloys with ultrahigh strength and excellent ductility simultaneously over a wide temperature range is crucial for developing high-temperature steam turbines [,,]. Recently, as a category of high-entropy alloys (HEAs), dual-phase high-entropy alloys (DP-HEAs) with a soft FCC phase and hard BCC (B2) phase have been reported to have excellent strength–ductility synergy at ambient temperature and high temperature [,,,,,,,,,], and thus have great potential to be used as steam turbine hot end components. Unfortunately, due to the rapid softening of the phase with the BCC structure at high temperatures, the yield strength of the alloy will significantly decrease [,,,,,]. Moreover, due to the weakness of grain boundaries and phase boundaries, the cracks initiate rapidly and propagate along the interface during high-temperature deformation, severely limiting the high-temperature application of FCC/B2 dual-phase high-entropy alloys [,,,,].

As we all know, the alloying of metals with certain specific elements can very effectively improve alloy properties through various strengthening methods such as precipitation strengthening, solution strengthening, and interface strengthening [,,,]. Hf is an essential alloying element for both the interface strengthening of superalloys and the strengthening of the Ni-Al B2 phase [,,,,,]. Recently, some studies have shown that adding a small amount of Hf to a single-phase FCC high-entropy alloy could improve the room-temperature mechanical property of the alloy without significantly reducing the ductility of the alloy through the precipitation of intermetallic compounds such as Ni7Hf2 and Laves phases [,]. However, these studies mainly focus on single-phase high-entropy alloys, and the addition of Hf is relatively large, usually more than one atom. Therefore, the effect of trace Hf addition on the properties of the alloy at room temperature and high temperature is worthy of in-depth investigation.

The strengthening effect of Hf on the alloy could be maintained at 600 °C, 800 °C, and 900 °C.At different high temperatures, the Hf0.5 alloy exhibited a higher strength and ductility than the Hf0 alloys. The outstanding high-temperature strength of the Hf0.5 alloy was attributed to the precipitation strengthening of the Hf-rich phase precipitated in the inner of the B2 phase. The excellent high-temperature ductility of the Hf0.5 alloy was attributed to the pinning effect of the Hf-rich phase that existed at grain and phase boundaries to boundary sliding during the high-temperature deformation.

Multiphase alloys with heterogeneous microstructures demonstrate excellent combination of strength and ductility, making them attractive for myriad structural applications [,,]. Recently, eutectic high entropy alloys (HEAs) with multiple solid solution phases have been the subject of extensive research due to their promise of overcoming the strength-ductility tradeoff seen in metals and conventional alloys [,,,,,,,]. The AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy represents a canonical example of an eutectic HEA with the lamellar arrangement of CoCrFe-rich L12 and AlNi-rich B2 phases [], which exhibit an excellent combination of strength and ductility at room temperature as well as exceptional strain hardening behavior that is largely retained up to 700 °C. Different processing routes have been utilized for achieving a wide range of microstructural features, resulting in outstanding mechanical properties and excellent corrosion resistance in these alloys. The ease of attaining ultrafine microstructure in directly cast eutectic HEAs is uncommon in conventional alloys [].
